analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to income above $400,000, including investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from July 11, 2023 until December 2024, was sent to two subcommittees two weeks before the Congress ended, and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, wages above a yearly ceiling (about $160,000) are not taxed for Social Security, and much investment income is taxed only lightly. This bill would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages up to $400,000, add a 1.2% tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000, and raise the tax on large investment income by 13.6% for people earning over $400,000 (17.4% total for trusts). It also closes a common workaround where owners of private businesses classify their work income as business profits to avoid payroll taxes. The new revenue would be routed directly into the Social Security trust funds and the Medicare hospital trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who pays into or draws from Social Security and Medicare: the bill would add revenue to the trust funds from the highest earners, extending their solvency and reducing pressure for future benefit cuts or retirement-age increases. It does not raise taxes on anyone earning under $400,000.

how_it_helps.text: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages between the current annual ceiling and $400,000, so high earners contribute beyond the current cap.
Adds a 1.2% tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for joint filers) for Medicare.
Raises the tax on net investment income by an additional 13.6% for individuals with income over $400,000, and sets the rate for trusts and estates at 17.4%.
Applies payroll tax to the pass-through business profits of owners earning more than $400,000, closing the treatment of owner work income as untaxed business profits.
Directs the new revenue into the Social Security old-age, survivors, and disability trust funds and the Medicare hospital insurance trust fund.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals earning over $400,000 (over $500,000 for couples), owners of large pass-through businesses such as partnerships and law firms, and trusts and estates with large investment income. No one earning under $400,000 pays anything under this bill.

drawbacks.text: High earners taxed between the current Social Security cap and $400,000 would not receive any additional Social Security benefits from those new contributions, since the bill changes only the tax side, not the benefit formula — a pay-more-without-more-benefit criticism its opponents would raise.

The combined rate on high-income investment income would rise to 17.4% (the existing 3.8% plus the new 13.6%), a large jump that critics argue would fall on retirees living off savings and on the owners of pass-through businesses, potentially discouraging investment.

The bill includes no independent budget score in the record, so the public does not know from the provided material exactly how much it would extend the trust funds' solvency or how quickly the revenue would arrive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and real: a new, dedicated revenue stream for programs that tens of millions of Americans rely on, paid entirely by the top sliver of earners. The cost is concentrated on households and business owners above $400,000, and the design has one genuine criticism — the middle band of new Social Security tax comes with no new benefits for the people paying it. On balance it is a straightforward solvency measure whose main risk is the unscored size of its impact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee when introduced and never got a markup or floor vote; in mid-December 2024, about two weeks before the Congress ended, it was sent to two subcommittees and died there.

narrative.text: Introduced on July 11, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax bills.

The bill's committee activity for the rest of the session was limited to referrals to the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Social Security on December 17, 2024, roughly two weeks before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote on the bill appears anywhere in its action history.
The bill attracted 2 cosponsors, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, large pass-through business owners, and trusts keep the current tax treatment, and the Social Security and Medicare trust funds go without the new revenue. Everyone drawing on those programs keeps the existing funding gap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoided the new taxes

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to the Ways and Means Committee, his own committee jurisdiction.

for.name: Two House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the entire session; sent it to two subcommittees only on December 17, 2024, two weeks before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor schedule for the first half of the session and never brought the bill up; it received no floor action at any point.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the record shows no Republican support; the bill also never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would reveal the full partisan split.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge funds, and other investment partnerships
industries.note: The bill applies payroll taxes to the pass-through business profits of owners earning over $400,000, ending the practice of classifying owner work income as business profits that escape payroll tax. Fund managers would pay materially more.

industries.industry: Law firms, consultancies, and other professional pass-through businesses
industries.note: Owners of S corporations, LLCs, and partnerships earning over $400,000 would owe payroll tax on income they currently receive as untaxed distributed profits.

industries.industry: Trusts and estates with large investment income
industries.note: The investment income tax rate for trusts and estates would rise from 3.8% to 17.4%.
Households with income over $400,000 would pay new payroll and investment income taxes under the bill; no household below that threshold pays anything.
